title: Teleskop NASA Jatuh di Langit Sumatra
question: Apa cahaya terang yang melesat dan pecah di langit Sumatra Utara pada malam 4 November 2026 — dan bagaimana kisah teleskop luar angkasa di baliknya?
audience: Penonton Indonesia yang suka kisah sains dan kejadian nyata: mereka mengikuti berita antariksa dari potongan-potongan pendek, dan film ini menyusun kisah utuhnya dalam satu tontonan.
promise: Penonton bisa menceritakan kembali: Swift adalah teleskop pemburu ledakan terbesar di alam semesta yang bekerja 22 tahun, jatuh perlahan karena atmosfer yang mengembang, gagal diselamatkan wahana robotik yang jatuh lebih dulu, dan pulang sebagai bola api di atas Sumatra tanpa mencelakai siapa pun.

facts.claim: Swift (Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory), NASA: launched 20 Nov 2004 on a Delta II from Cape Canaveral; planned 2-year mission; served nearly 22 years.
Three instruments working as one team: BAT (gamma-ray), XRT (X-ray), UVOT (UV/optical).
Results: more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts detected; at least 1,400 supernovae studied; data in about 7,000 scientific papers; archive about 12 TB (and over 1.5 million UVOT images).

'Swift' means fast: after BAT catches a burst the spacecraft slews autonomously in about 20–75 seconds to aim XRT and UVOT; on average one burst every 2–3 days. Gamma-ray bursts are the most powerful explosions in the universe since the Big Bang.
Renamed the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory in January 2018 for its principal investigator Neil Gehrels, who died in 2017.
Swift's orbit was about 600 km up, one lap about 96.6 minutes.
The recent solar maximum heated and expanded Earth's upper atmosphere, increasing drag and accelerating Swift's orbital decay.

Rescue: NASA awarded Katalyst Space Technologies about US$30 million (Sept 2025) for the Swift Boost mission; LINK launched 3 July 2026 on a Pegasus XL (that rocket's final flight); the plan was to grapple Swift with robotic arms and raise it back to about 600 km. LINK was designed, built and launched in under a year; Swift was never designed to be captured.
facts.source: The Space Review, article 5299; space.skyrocket.de (Link SRM); logikgear.

facts.claim: Late July 2026 LINK lost two of its three reaction wheels and spun uncontrolled at up to about 9 degrees per second; engineers slowed the spin to about 1.47 degrees per second by 5 August, but steering with thrusters burned the propellant meant for the boost.
On 19 August 2026 NASA and Katalyst called off the capture and boost; LINK still flew to within 12–15 km of Swift and tested its robotic arms and thrusters, but never touched it.
LINK itself re-entered the atmosphere and burned up in September 2026 — the rescuer fell first.
On 20 October 2026 Swift made its last science observations from about 275 km (171 miles), where drag already prevented steady pointing; NASA ended the mission days later (23 October 2026).
Re-entry: 4 November 2026, 07:39 EST = 12:39 UTC = 19:39 WIB, over North Sumatra at about 3.4 degrees north, 98.6 degrees east (U.S. Space Force); the spacecraft broke apart and most of it burned up.
facts.source: NASA Swift blog via technology.org / tech-insider.org, Nov 2026.

facts.claim: Entry speed about 28,000 km/h (orbital velocity about 7.8 km/s), more than twenty times the speed of sound (derived: about Mach 22.7 at sea level). Some dense components may have survived the entry; no debris was ever confirmed found.
facts.source: Derived from orbital velocity; NASA expectation via technology.org; tech-insider.org (no confirmed debris recovery).

facts.claim: NASA's pre-entry estimate of the chance of anyone on Earth being harmed was about 1 in 2,100. In the event there were no reports of damage and no injuries; people in the region filmed a bright streak in the night sky.
facts.source: NASA via technology.org; worldofnow (NASA's farewell reported no debris impact or injury).

acts.title: Malam Itu di Sumatra
acts.goal: Open on the night itself: a bright streak breaks apart over North Sumatra, people film it, and the question lands — what was that light? The answer: a NASA space telescope coming home.

acts.title: Pemburu Ledakan Terbesar
acts.goal: Meet Swift: launched in 2004 for two years, worked nearly twenty-two; three telescopes as one team hunting gamma-ray bursts, the biggest explosions in the universe, slewing in under seventy-five seconds.

acts.title: Jatuh Perlahan
acts.goal: Explain the slow fall as a mechanism: a whisper of air at 600 km, a swelling atmosphere at solar maximum, and the spiral in which lower means faster — with no engine of its own to climb back.

acts.title: Penolong yang Jatuh Lebih Dulu
acts.goal: Tell the rescue whole: Katalyst's LINK, built in under a year, the grapple-and-boost plan, the lost reaction wheels, the spin, the fuel spent saving itself, the August cancellation — and LINK burning up first, in September.

acts.title: Malam Terakhir
acts.goal: The last look at the sky on 20 October from 275 km, the mission's end, then the night of 4 November 2026, 19:39 WIB: entry over North Sumatra at 28,000 km/h, the fireball the hook opened with, the one-in-2,100 risk — and nobody harmed.

acts.title: Yang Tertinggal di Bumi
acts.goal: Land the legacy: the telescope is gone, its 12 TB archive and ~7,000 papers remain and are still read; close on the line to remember.
